chunks.content: 1 INTRODUCTION Generating and translating high‐quality evidence is integral to providing safe and effective medication management for residents of aged care homes. Despite this, residents of aged care homes are often under‐represented in research, with only 2% of studies involving older people being conducted in the aged care home setting, resulting in evidence gaps. , These gaps present a challenge to clinicians because evidence from clinical trials and observational studies on community‐dwelling older adults cannot necessarily be extrapolated to residents of aged care homes. Residents of aged care homes are often older and frailer with higher rates of cognitive impairment and polypharmacy. This means that residents may be particularly vulnerable to adverse drug events and have different treatment benefits and risks than robust community‐dwelling older adults. , These factors may necessitate different strategies for evidence generation and translation. Evidence translation can depend on the nature of evidence generation, and vice versa. Considering barriers and facilitators to evidence translation when designing research can help facilitate the uptake and sustainability of evidence‐based interventions. , , Previous systematic reviews report challenges of conducting research and translating evidence in aged care homes. , , A recent scoping review found tailored education and peer champions are successful for implementing interventions. Knowledge brokers can act as peer champions to implement tailored strategies for knowledge translation. , To our knowledge, no reviews have explored generating and translating evidence in the aged care setting. Existing reviews have been conducted in acute care, outpatient and primary care settings, which are not specific to aged care homes. , Medication management in this narrative review refers to the prescribing, dispensing, administration and monitoring of medications. It consists of activities and processes that ensure the safe and effective use of medications at each episode of care. This narrative review will explore opportunities and challenges for generating and translating evidence for safe and effective medication management in aged care homes with key examples related to prevalent and high‐risk medications. A non‐systematic search of bibliometric databases including PubMed, Embase and Google Scholar was conducted across the domains of aged care homes (e.g. ‘nursing home’, ‘long‐term care’, ‘residential aged care’, ‘aged care home’), medications (e.g. ‘medication’, ‘medicine’, ‘medication management’), and evidence generation and translation (e.g. ‘barrier’, ‘facilitator’, ‘randomised control trial’, ‘cohort study’, ‘implementation’, ‘knowledge translation’). Key articles that addressed generating and translating evidence in aged care were included. Reference lists of relevant studies were also reviewed to identify key articles for inclusion. 1.1 Need for evidence in relation to outcomes prioritized by residents, carers and aged care provider organizations Few studies assess non‐pharmacological outcomes integral to the holistic care of residents of aged care homes. These include outcomes such as emotions, mood, or the impact on social life that are prioritized by people living with Alzheimer's disease. The Lancet Commission on Long Term‐Care for Older Persons has recognized the need for better integration of medical and social services to allow residents to remain engaged in meaningful and fulfilling activities. Nearly two‐thirds of participants in the World Health Organization (WHO) Research Priorities to Reduce the Global Burden of Dementia initiative prioritized the need for better study outcome measures. Residents of aged care homes may have different goals of care when compared to robust community‐dwelling older adults. For example, residents with limited life expectancy may prioritize symptom management rather than long‐term prevention. Older adults living with dementia may prioritize outcomes such as quality of life, pill burden, falls risk and avoidance of hospitalizations when deciding whether or not to take antihypertensive medications. A systematic review reported patient involvement in developing core outcome sets increased the likelihood of including quality of life outcomes. Involving residents and carers in selecting research outcomes may help overcome the gaps between common clinical trial outcomes and those prioritized by residents. Including residents and informal carers in Guideline Development Groups may be important because residents may have different treatment preferences to clinicians or care home staff. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) evidence‐to‐decision framework provides a mechanism to consider resident and carer perspectives when developing clinical practice guidelines. Despite this, resident involvement in evidence‐synthesis and clinical decision‐making remains limited, although there is some evidence that this is changing. A study involving aged care home staff and resident co‐design of an aged care home service to improve resident wellbeing highlighted the value of resident involvement, reporting strengthened resident‐staff relationships, resident reported satisfaction and improved staff capacity to advocate for resident needs and values. The SPRINT trial reported intensive blood pressure lowering to <120 mmHg reduced the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality compared to blood pressure <140 mmHg in participants aged ≥75 years. While SPRINT is often used to justify antihypertensive prescribing for older people, SPRINT excluded people living in aged care homes and those living with dementia. In contrast, the PARTAGE study demonstrated combination antihypertensive therapy in residents of aged care homes with blood pressure <130 mmHg was associated with a higher risk of mortality. Another example of clinical uncertainty relates to prescribing bisphosphonates for osteoporosis. Qualitative research suggests clinicians are uncertain about prescribing and deprescribing for people with dementia, limited mobility and in the context of limited bone densitometry undertaken in the aged care home setting. Most international osteoporosis guidelines ( n = 29, 69%) refer to deprescribing of bisphosphonates in the context of drug holidays, which are not advised for patients at high‐risk of fractures and most of these guidelines do not make specific deprescribing recommendations for residents with limited life expectancy. High‐risk medications including warfarin, insulins, oral antiplatelet agents and oral hypoglycaemic agents are not generally classified as potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) but are implicated in two‐thirds of all adverse drug event related emergency department presentations of older adults in the United States (US). Glucose‐lowering medications are important for achieving glycaemic control but 5–86% of residents are potentially over‐treated and 1–35% potentially under‐treated for diabetes in aged care homes, suggesting a high degree of variability in pharmacological management of diabetes. This highlights the importance of healthcare professionals and care staff being aware of these high‐risk medications, in addition to PIMs, and the importance of ensuring both resident and system‐level processes are in place to minimize the risk of errors and medication‐related harm. Lack of aged care specific evidence‐based guidelines has been described as a barrier to deprescribing. Process evaluations of deprescribing interventions help generate evidence on contextual factors integral to deprescribing. , Development of deprescribing guidelines could be aided by international deprescribing networks such as those established in Canada, Australia, US and Europe and national deprescribing policies. , Medication‐related clinical decision support tools synthesize evidence‐based recommendations to inform medication prescribing decisions, usually at the point of care. Many clinical decision support tools and explicit criteria for PIMs, such as Beers Criteria and the Screening Tool of Older Persons' Prescriptions (STOPP) and Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment (START) criteria are not specific to the aged care home or end‐of‐life care settings. Despite being originally proposed for residents in aged care homes, Beers Criteria are now intended for all adults aged 65 years and older except in hospice and end‐of‐life care settings. A study conducted in the US highlighted the need for consensus recommendations for appropriate prescribing in residents living with advanced dementia, to decrease polypharmacy and minimize the use of medications that are high‐risk or of minimal benefit. Identifying residents most at‐risk of preventable medication‐related harm in aged care homes is complicated because the implicated medications are not necessarily inappropriate for all residents. A range of multidisciplinary staff are involved in medication management. For example, care staff spend considerable time with residents and have an important influence on medication decision‐making. Engaging all stakeholders in medication management interventions may facilitate antipsychotic deprescribing in residents living with dementia. A qualitative study involving United Kingdom (UK) aged care homes reported modifications were required to make deprescribing tools suitable for the aged care setting. A systematic mapping review of RCTs reported that there were at least 292 RCTs conducted in aged care homes internationally between 1974 and 2009, with half of these studies published between 2003 and 2009. These studies focused on behaviour, prescribing and malnutrition. Of 397 intervention studies in aged care homes from 2015 to 2022, the most common intervention related to medication management ( n = 56, 14.1%). It is unclear if the number of studies conducted in the aged care home setting has continued to increase in recent years. 2.1 RCTs RCTs are regarded as the gold standard study design for evaluating medication efficacy and safety. This is because randomization minimizes bias by balancing known and unknown confounding factors across study groups. Despite residents of aged care homes being among the most vulnerable population groups, and the first to be vaccinated in many countries, <10% of participants in COVID‐19 vaccine clinical trials were aged 65 years or older and <1% were 85 years or older. Of 39 RCTs conducted in Australian aged care homes from 2000 to 2018, the most common focus areas were dementia, falls prevention and mental health. Most RCTs were not focused on medication efficacy or safety and few assessed resident quality of life as recommended by the Lancet Commission on Long Term‐Care for Older Persons. , Traditional RCTs often have a rigid study design that can be challenging to implement for investigating medication management interventions in an aged care home setting. This is because routines may be inflexible, staff may have competing clinical care priorities between residents, and residents may experience fluctuations in cognitive function and behaviours. Investigators will need to consider these factors when obtaining consent, undertaking data collection and resident follow‐up. RCTs that measure outcomes prioritized by residents may not provide evidence on hard endpoints typically measured in RCTs. However, novel trial designs such as stepped‐wedge and helix counterbalanced designs have been used to overcome the limitations of traditional RCTs such as small sample sizes, need to adjust for aged care home characteristics and participant drop‐out following randomization into the control rather than intervention group. , , 2.2 Conducting observational studies High‐quality observational studies can also help address the evidence‐gap arising from under‐representation of residents of aged care homes in RCTs. Cohort and case–control study designs permit analyses for large and generalizable resident samples. For example, a large cohort study based on a US Medicare aged care home sample with 2‐year follow up reported similar rates of injurious falls and cardiovascular events following commencement of a first‐line antihypertensive in residents with limited life expectancy. Observational studies also allow for investigation of important outcomes that may not occur in the context of RCTs that have small sample sizes and short durations. For example, a nested case–control study involving aged care home residents found that current use of antipsychotic medications appeared to be associated with a slightly increased risk of hip fracture compared to nonusers (adjusted odds ratio = 1.26, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.05–1.52). Cohort and case–control studies are also relatively low cost compared to RCTs. Methods such as propensity score matching and inverse probability of treatment weighting can be used in these studies to account for possible bias and confounding. However, prevalent‐user designs that involve cross‐sectional medication exposure assessment may be particularly problematic for analytical studies in the aged care home setting because clinicians may selectively deprescribe medications for the frailest subset of residents who are at highest risk of adverse events, hospitalization or death. This means that nonusers of the medication under investigation may comprise both never‐users and those who discontinued (e.g. due to lack of efficacy, adverse events or change of treatment goals). Although new‐user designs overcome some of the limitations of prevalent‐user designs, new‐user designs are challenging to implement in the aged care home setting as residents are often long‐term users of the medication under investigation prior to entry into the aged care home. Drug utilization studies are important for identifying areas for quality improvement initiatives. For example, a 2024 repeated cross‐sectional study reported an increase in antidepressant use among residents of aged care homes. Understanding the strengths and limitations of different data sources is particularly relevant to the aged care home setting because medications are often charted for regular or as‐needed administration, may be medical or nurse‐initiated, or be unable to be consumed as intended (e.g. due to swallowing difficulties). When interpreting medication prevalence estimates from drug use studies, clinicians and policymakers should consider the data source and exposure time window. The Neurological and Mental Health Global Epidemiology Network (NeuroGEN) is an international big‐data platform used to facilitate high‐quality observational studies. NeuroGEN comprises 15 databases with data for >320 million individuals. International multidatabase pharmacoepidemiological research using common study protocols and common data models can improve generalizability of research findings. 2.3 Barriers and facilitators to generating evidence in the aged care home setting Research in the aged care home setting considers resident‐, facility‐ and system‐level factors that may influence the uptake, conduct and success of the research (Figure ). , , , , , These factors may be specific to aged care home, and therefore researchers need to invest time into understanding each local context. Reported rates of resident recruitment for prospective studies have ranged from 0–42%. Obtaining ethical written informed consent from residents, particularly those with cognitive impairment or their carers, can be resource intensive and require multiple conversations at different times or days to accommodate resident and carer schedules or health status. , Successful recruitment typically involves allocating appropriate written and staffing‐related resources for these conversations, including staff attending in‐person and the development of concise, lay‐language study materials. Not allocating adequate resources for resident recruitment could lead to under‐representation of residents with dementia who may not be able to provide written informed consent themselves. Also, recruitment may be maximized by providing information for residents, carers and aged care home staff in different formats, for example, information sessions, posters and videos. , In the SIMPLER trial, written information for residents and carers was prepared in accordance with the Dementia Australia Guide to Dementia Friendly Language, and the study nurses who recruited residents were trained in Dementia Australia Let us talk tips. Cognitive screening tools such as the Evaluation to Sign Consent measure and Brief Interview for Mental Status (BIMS) can be used to initially screen resident ability to consent to participate in research. Evaluation to Sign Consent has demonstrated some evidence of reliability and validity. An observational study compared BIMS scores with aged care home staff assessments of resident capacity and found that the higher the BIMS score (indicating greater intact cognition), the more likely the aged care home staff were to assess the resident as being able to consent ( P < .001). Although cognitive screening tools may support initial screening for recruitment, they should not substitute rigorous assessment of a resident's ability to provide full consent. In addition to supporting resident involvement in research, establishing effective and genuine partnerships with aged care organizations and aged care home staff is critical for success. Engaging aged care providers as research partners in the conceptualization and design phase can help ensure that the research addresses shared priorities, and that appropriate and acceptable structures and processes are put in place to address potential industry‐wide barriers such as workloads, staff turnover and staff knowledge on the importance of research. While providing clinical care is the highest priority for aged care organizations, research has an important role in improving the quality and efficiency of care. High‐quality clinical care and research are not mutually exclusive and delivering high‐quality clinical care is dependent on access to robust evidence. It is possible that different aged care organizations place a different level of emphasis on research and therefore the results of research conducted with one organization may not necessarily be generalizable to the wider aged care sector. Increasing use of electronic point‐of‐care systems and linked data may also facilitate more timely and granular data access, and may help to reduce the burden of data collection. 3 TRANSLATING EVIDENCE Efficient and timely translation of evidence into practice can support the delivery of high‐quality, evidence‐based care. Poor uptake of evidence and clinical practice guidelines is a known barrier to high‐quality care across all health settings, yet research into strategies specific to the aged care home setting is lacking, particularly in relation to improving medication management. Poor uptake of evidence and clinical practice guidelines is a known barrier to high‐quality care across all health settings, yet research into strategies specific to the aged care home setting is lacking, particularly in relation to improving medication management. A 2022 overview of systematic reviews of strategies for implementing clinical practice guidelines found only 4 (11%) studies were conducted in the aged care home setting. 3.1 Strategies for facilitating evidence translation Effective translation helps to ensure delivery of consistent, evidence‐based care. Several strategies can be implemented to facilitate evidence translation in aged care homes (Figure ). , , , , Sustained implementation of guideline recommendations is challenging, with current literature reporting only one‐third of guideline recommendations are sustained over‐time. Evidence translation strategies can be guided by a knowledge translation or implementation framework such as the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) , and Integrated Promoting Action on Research Implementation in Health Services (i‐PARIHS) framework. Application of these frameworks requires a sound understanding of aged care management structures governance, local policy and procedures and staff and resident characteristics. A process evaluation study of a cluster RCT performed in Dutch aged care homes applied CFIR and found that peer champions aided the implementation of an electronic health record tool for empirical treatment of urinary tract infections. Local factors such as time constraints, staffing levels and access to resources have been identified as common barriers to clinical practice guideline implementation in the aged care home setting. These barriers may be addressed through achieving leadership buy‐in and ensuring adequate financial resources for implementation. Adequate staffing with an appropriate skill‐mix to accommodate research tasks should be accounted for in the research budget. 3.1.1 Audit and feedback Audit and feedback is a widely used strategy for implementation of new evidence into clinical practice. Audit and feedback reviews current clinical practice against explicit standards and uses this data to develop, implement and evaluate quality improvement initiatives. A Cochrane review assessed the effects of audit and feedback on professional practice and healthcare outcomes and reported a median 4.3% (interquartile range 0.5–16%) absolute improvement in healthcare professional adherence to the desired standard of practice. Repeating audit and feedback cycles has the potential to generate a cumulative incremental improvement to professional practice or healthcare outcomes. An audit and feedback intervention addressing high‐risk prescriptions in Canadian aged care homes reported a good return of investment of 1.02 (95% CI 0.51–1.93) for every C$1 spent on the intervention. Furthermore, effective provision of context‐specific feedback is important for practice change. This may include repeat feedback in both written and verbal format with explicit targets and an action plan. 3.1.2 Quality indicators Quality indicators are one method of auditing clinical care in aged care homes. Mandatory reporting of aged care home quality indicators has been in place in the US since 2002 and more recently was implemented in Australia in 2019. , Guidelines such as the 2021 Society for Post‐Acute and Long‐Term Care Medicine Pain Management Guideline and 2019 Infectious Diseases Society of America Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Asymptomatic Bacteriuria are being published with quality indicators that can be used by aged care homes and healthcare professionals to audit concordance with best practice. , While these indicators can be useful for auditing, the governance structures supporting a feedback loop to inform iterative practice change is often missing or is reliant on proactive individuals. 3.1.3 Local action plans Local action plans can be informed by audits and quality indicator data. A pragmatic RCT in Canadian aged care homes demonstrated that feedback approaches involving goal setting and written action plans were effective in improving care aide involvement in communication about resident care. Furthermore, developing and implementing local action plans through a dementia care quality improvement collaborative increased community, hospital and aged care clinician self‐reported guideline adherence by 41.2% ( P = .012, CI 1.08–1.87). Clinicians applied the plan‐do‐study‐act model to develop their own implementation plan to generate iterative improvements in guideline adherence. Local action plans created by individuals or collaboratives with a comprehensive understanding of the local context may have the potential to improve guideline adherence, particularly if used in conjunction with other knowledge translation strategies such as audit and feedback. 3.1.4 Education and training Education and training builds the capacity of staff to address existing knowledge gaps but requires organizational support to encourage and reinforce learning and provide additional paid work time. Academic detailing is a form of education outreach that involves synthesizing evidence into a simplified format and presenting this to a clinician via interactive discussion. A Cochrane review of education outreach on professional practice and healthcare outcomes reported a 5.6% (interquartile range 3.0–9.0%) median adjusted risk difference in compliance with desired practice. The adjusted risk differences for prescribing were highly consistent, but were variable for other types of professional activities. An antimicrobial stewardship programme, which delivered education and training to aged care home clinicians on antimicrobial prescribing and the use of antimicrobial stewardship tools reported a significant 16% reduction in resistance to fluoroquinolone antibiotic ofloxacin ( P = .004). Clinician unfamiliarity with clinical practice guidelines or preference to use own pre‐existing knowledge has been highlighted as a common barrier to uptake. , , Provision of education and training to aged care home staff can promote awareness, interpretation and application of guidelines. Companion resources such as point of care checklists to support clinical decision making and concise guideline summaries may facilitate guideline awareness, familiarity and adherence. There may be benefit in producing consumer resources in different languages to support evidence uptake in culturally and linguistically diverse communities within the same country. For example, Australia's new companion guide accompanying The Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Appropriate Use of Psychotropic Medications in People Living with Dementia and in Residential Aged Care has been translated into simplified and traditional Mandarin, Vietnamese, Greek and Italian. 3.2 Knowledge brokers to facilitate knowledge translation Knowledge brokers are individuals or groups who act as intermediaries to move knowledge from those who produce it (e.g. guideline developers) to those that use it (e.g. clinicians). They act as knowledge managers, linkage agents and capacity builders. Knowledge brokers have been primarily used in the hospital setting to facilitate guideline implementation, but are increasingly being used in the aged care home setting. , They may use a variety of knowledge translation strategies, including education, local action plans, development of guideline implementation tools, and audit and feedback, to build the capacity and capability of staff and systems to implement new guidelines. Knowledge brokers have been shown to improve guideline adherence in up to 63% of studies, but there is a paucity of evidence on their effectiveness and cost‐effectiveness in the aged care home setting. 4 FUTURE DIRECTIONS 4.1 International knowledge sharing There is increasing recognition of the value of international research collaboration. This has been highlighted by the United Nations and WHO through the 2021–2030 Decade of Healthy Aging. In 2021, WHO launched the Global Dementia Observatory Knowledge Exchange Platform. Through this initiative, resources submitted to the Platform are peer‐reviewed and mapped to strategic action areas of the Global Action Plan on the Public Health Response to Dementia 2017–2025. Other initiatives to share knowledge between countries include the Guidelines International Network library and registry of guidelines in development. Specific research networks, such as the UK National Institute for Health and Care Research—Enabling Research in Care Homes (ENRICH) programme, enable knowledge sharing to help to identify areas of best practice and opportunities for improvement. Understanding the value of specific evidence for informing policy and practice is often dependent on appreciating similarities and differences in aged care systems across states and countries. A recent study that investigated transferability of aged care research between 7 countries (Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, UK and USA) reported that these countries were superficially comparable in terms of the percentage gross domestic product spent on aged care homes and proportion of residents living with dementia. However, the lack of standardization on how aged care home data are reported compromises opportunities for international comparisons. Core outcome sets developed with resident and carer input may provide opportunities to measure outcomes that are prioritized by residents and support national and international comparisons across different studies. 4.2 Optimizing use of technology Digitalization and increasing access to routinely collected administrative health data (e.g. pharmacy claims and hospital records) are creating new opportunities for conducting cohort and case control studies in aged care homes. The Long‐Term Care Data Cooperative funded by the National Institute on Aging links resident electronic health records with Medicare claims in the USA. In August 2022, this cooperative included 1000 aged care homes with the aim to increase access to timely clinical data for research. Data linkage may provide new opportunities for analysing outcomes prioritized by residents and carers, for example, cognition, physical function and behaviours. The Long‐Term Care Data Cooperative funded by the National Institute on Aging links resident electronic health records with Medicare claims in the USA. In August 2022, this cooperative included 1000 aged care homes with the aim to increase access to timely clinical data for research. Data linkage may provide new opportunities for analysing outcomes prioritized by residents and carers, for example, cognition, physical function and behaviours. New information technology infrastructure that enables the use of real‐time data analytics may support clinical decision‐making. Real‐time predictive analytic dashboards embedded into aged care homes have been developed, allowing for timely integration of resident health information. Web‐based tools such as The Goal‐directed Medication review Electronic Decision Support System (G‐MEDSS) is an example of a digital clinical decision support system tool that addresses the need for resident medication goals of care to be integrated into clinical reviews. 5 CONCLUSION Developing and strengthening strategies for generating and translating evidence in the aged care home setting is imperative to bridge existing evidence gaps for safe and effective medication management and improved resident outcomes. Facilitators of evidence generation and translation into the aged care home setting could guide opportunities to facilitate robust research. These facilitators include effective partnerships with aged care homes, establishing research networks and embedded knowledge brokers. Integrating outcomes prioritized by residents and aged care organizations into future research and resident involvement in evidence‐synthesis can ensure medication management strategies developed are tailored to residents' needs, supporting improved quality of life and preventing medication‐related harms. Introduction Postoperative delirium (POD), which is an acute and transitory brain condition, includes focus problems, disruptions in consciousness, and notable oscillations in cognitive function. POD is defined as delirium that manifests within a week following surgery and mainly occurs within 24–72 hours [ ] . HIGHLIGHTS There was just one type of patient in this trial, and there were very few intervening variables that could have affected the result. Although POD typically occurs in the first 72 hours after surgery, we followed up patients to discharge or postoperative day 5 to evaluate the entire postoperative period in which delirium is diagnosed. We had a high rate of in-person delirium assessment completion, which is challenging, with a rigorous protocol evaluating for delirium twice daily to capture the waxing and waning nature of the disorder. The number of elderly people undergoing arthroscopy and joint replacement surgeries in China is increasing as the population ages. However, POD is one of the most prevalent postoperative complications after orthopedic joint replacement surgery, occurring in 4–54.3% of elderly people after joint replacement surgery [ , ] . In addition to extending hospital stays, increasing costs, and necessitating specialized care after discharge, POD also increases the risk of complications such as pressure ulcers, dementia, pulmonary infections, urinary incontinence, and impaired joint function recovery immediately after surgery. It even increases the risk of death [ – ] . Thus, medical professionals must be diligent in preventing POD. Delirium has a complicated and multifaceted etiology [ , ] . Current research indicates that POD may be related to the mitochondrial dysfunction caused by anesthesia or surgery [ – ] . It has also been suggested that the restoration of mitochondrial activity can relieve postoperative cognitive impairment [ – ] . Considering that delirium and cognitive impairment are related and share common triggers, we speculate that focusing on mitochondria could be a potential way to prevent older patients from developing POD. The application of methylene blue (MB) in some surgical procedures has been considered safe. Studies have shown that MB can improve brain metabolism and restore mitochondrial function as a redox mediator in the electron transfer chain [ , ] . Moreover, MB can swiftly penetrate the blood‒brain barrier, infiltrate cerebral tissue, and accumulate in the mitochondria and cytoplasm of neurons [ ] . So we hypothesize that infusion of 2 mg/kg of MB within 60 minutes after induction of anesthesia can effectively reduce the incidence of POD (assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method scale) in elderly joint replacement patients without increasing the incidence of perioperative adverse events (AEs). Therefore, we designed this randomized controlled clinical trial to investigate whether MB can reduce the incidence of POD in elderly patients undergoing joint replacement surgery. Materials and methods This single-blind randomized and controlled trial followed the CONSORT criteria [ ] and the TITAN Guidelines [ ] . This clinical study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the hospital on 3 July 2023 and registered at the China Clinical Trial Center on 27 July 2023. After providing the participants with oral and written information about the study, written informed consent was obtained from the patients or a member of their immediate family. Patients recruitment All elderly patients scheduled to undergo joint replacement surgery in the surgical unit underwent preoperative screening with the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) scales. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) underwent elective joint replacement surgery under general anesthesia; (2) were aged ≥ 65 years; and (3) were willing to complete the neuropsychological assessment and were accessible for in-person follow-up interviews. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) preoperative dementia, severe depression, or severe psychological or neurological conditions; (2) allergy to 6-phospho-glucose dehydrogenase absence (favism) or hypersensitivity to MB; (3) drug or alcohol abuse or taking medications that may result in drug reactions, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors; (4) prior major brain injury; (5) emergency surgery; (6) serious medical conditions (such as severe liver or renal dysfunction, severe pulmonary hypertension, heart failure, and respiratory failure); (7) inability to complete scale assessments (such as significant sight, hearing, or linguistic impairments); (8) participation in other experimental studies within 3 months; and (9) preoperative MMSE score: illiterate MMSE < 17 points; primary school (≤6 years of education): MMSE < 20 points; and secondary school or above (>6 years of education): MMSE < 24 points. The withdrawal criteria were as follows: (1) severe AEs such as massive bleeding or intraoperative rescue and (2) admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) after surgery. Randomization and blinding The eligible individuals were assigned to the MB group or the control group (1:1). A researcher used basic randomization with numbers produced by SPSS software. Each sequentially numbered envelope contained the grouping, which was stored in an opaque and sealed envelope. When the participants entered the surgical area, the anesthesiologist opened the envelope and administered the intervention as planned appropriately, so the anesthesiologist was not blinded to the grouping. Patients were not blinded to the grouping, which may be predicted by the blue color of the urine. The urine bags of each individual were wrapped in a black plastic bag after surgery, and the patient’s family members were told not to inform the patients and postoperative follow-up staff of the color of urine until the urine tubes were removed. As a result, this clinical investigation was single-blind, randomized, and controlled. POD is characterized by a rapid onset and a fluctuating course. The symptoms typically manifest in episodes and start 24–72 hours following surgery [ ] . Here, we assessed the incidence of delirium in all patients for 5 consecutive days. The frequency of POD among these patients was 14.3%, comparable to earlier findings [ ] , with 8.3% of patients in the MB group and 20.4% of patients in the control group. Moreover, we observed that the majority of POD cases were hypoactive delirium (58.1%), a subtype of delirium characterized by symptoms of lethargy, stillness, immobility, and cognitive dissociation that is frequently disregarded in clinical settings. The outcomes of this research are in line with prior findings [ ] . The clinically “silent” hypoactive type may be more fatal than the hyperactive type [ ] , but the severity of delirium in the present study was milder. One month following surgery, the short half-life of MB may account for the lack of a statistically significant difference in TICS-m scores between the two groups. More research is still needed to explore the effects of varying MB delivery times and doses on POD development and delayed neurocognitive recovery. MB acts directly on the central nervous system, and its effect on the maintenance of and recovery from general anesthesia has been less studied. Previous research has indicated that administering a 5 mg/kg MB intravenous infusion 1 hour before surgery can decrease the intraoperative propofol maintenance dose and prolong recovery [ ] . According to the outcomes of the present study, there was no delay in postoperative anesthesia recovery in the two groups; however, the recovery time in the MB group was marginally longer than that in the control group. Nonetheless, there was no statistically significant difference in the intraoperative maintenance dose of propofol between the two groups. This may be due to differences in the anesthesia management protocols used during the operation. First, intraoperative propofol infusion did not implement target-controlled infusion during the anesthesia maintenance period. Second, we used to increase the concentration of inhaled anesthetics to adjust for increases in patients’ heart rates and blood pressure without recording the dosage of inhaled anesthetics. Consequently, more research is still required to fully understand the mechanism and connection between MB and anesthetics. The CRS-R reflects the patient’s state of consciousness through six behavioral aspects: visual, auditory, motor, verbal, communication, and arousal. It can be used for ongoing evaluation and is simple to use, so the CRS-R scale was used in this study to evaluate the consciousness of patients during recovery from general anesthesia. The results indicated that there was no statistically significant difference in CRS-R scores between 10 and 20 minutes after extubation, suggesting that MB could temporarily prolong patient recovery but did not affect the recovery of consciousness during the recovery period. The other side effects were not significantly different between the two groups. Introduction The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that the proportion of people over 60 years old will have doubled by 2050. This age group will account for more than two billion people by 2050, compared to 900 million in 2015 ( ). By general comparison, the Swiss population of older adults has a good general health status ( ). However, age-related biological changes including but not limited to sarcopenia, reduced abilities in walking, balance and coordination, sight disorders, cognitive decline and comorbidities are risk factors associated with a sharp increase in falls prevalence. For example, in Switzerland, prevalence over the population increased from 21% in 2002 to 26% in 2017 ( ). Polypharmacy and home hazards may also enhance this risk ( ; ; ). Worldwide, 28% to 35% of people over 64 years and 32% to 42% of those over 70 suffer of a fall each year. This phenomenon raises with age and level of frailty ( ). Fatal but also non-fatal injuries amongst older adults over 65 years old are mainly attributable to falls ( ). Of the 36 million falls in older adults in the United States of America, 20% will have severe consequences such as fractures or head injuries ( ). Those can strongly impact people’s quality of life, health and lifestyle ( ). Indeed, 21% to 85% of victims of a fall will experience physical, functional, psychological and social changes ( ). Therefore, a fear of falling can arise, with negative consequences on physical and functional well-being ( ), and a heightened risk of future falls ( ; ). The falls consequences remain various and can be far-reaching: chronic pain, loss of mobility and autonomy, anxiety, long-term hospitalisations or placements in healthcare centres ( ; ). This can lead to significant direct financial costs. For example, in Switzerland, hospitalisation for a hip fracture costs CHF 15,000 ( ), and a year spent in an institution around CHF 100,000 per person ( ; ). In addition, indirect costs, including losses due to premature death, morbidity or disability, unpaid activities, care services, but also intangible costs related to pain and loss of quality of life, are also attributable to falls ( ). Globally, the socio-economic costs (material and immaterial) related to falls amounted to CHF 14.7 billion in 2017 in Switzerland ( ). Guidelines ( ; ; ; ; ), clinical guidance statements ( ), and systematic reviews ( ; ; ; ), have emphasised the effectiveness of multifactorial assessments for determining the risk of falling and for informing the implementation of personalised fall prevention strategies ( ). It is recommended that older adults over 65 years old should regularly (at least once per year) be assessed for fall risk, e.g. by asking about their fall histories, frequencies, contexts and characteristics ( ). As movement specialists, physiotherapists constitute a primary point of intervention in preventing falls ( ). They can, for example, inform physicians and home care agencies regarding fall risk factors ( ). Effective fall prevention interventions involve three main steps. First, the screening enables detection of increased fall risk. For example, inquiring regularly about falls history can help to identify individuals at higher risk of future falls. Second, intrinsic and extrinsic factors are investigated through additional assessments such as medication review, mobility level, posture, blood pressure, vision, gait and balance, lower extremity joint function, neurologic and cognitive function, muscular strength, proprioception, reflexes, and/or environmental assessment. Finally, appropriate interventions aim to reduce the rate of falls and the severity of injury. Multidimensional individualised exercise programs are considered a reliable method of preventing falls in older persons ( ; ; ). However, little is known about the current practices of physiotherapists concerning fall prevention. To our knowledge, there are no published data on the implementation of fall risk assessment guidelines by physiotherapists in Switzerland. To ensure our profession provides guideline-recommended care for older adults, it is necessary to review current clinical practices in screening fall risk in patients over 65 years old. Therefore, this online survey sought to evaluate to what extent physiotherapists carry out fall risk assessments as the first step towards a fall prevention intervention in the population of community-dwelling older adults in Switzerland. The aim was to determine whether current practices are in line with current recommendations. After identifying barriers and facilitators to fall risk assessment, recommendations on appropriate clinical resources and targeted training will be proposed. Statistics The distributions of the continuous variables were analysed visually, and median, interquartile range, minimal and maximal values were reported. Categorical variables were summarised with absolute and relative frequencies. 95% confidence intervals were reported to document the statistical precision of the estimates. The significance level was set at p<0.05 for all tests. Differences between participants with more than 10% missing values and those with fewer missing values were compared with non-parametric tests for continuous variables and with Chi-squared tests for frequency tables. Cohen’s d effect size was calculated for continuous variables. An effect size of 0.2 was considered a slight difference, 0.5 a moderate difference and 0.8 a significant difference. Cramer’s V effect sizes were calculated for categorical variables, where 0.1 was considered small, 0.3 moderate and 0.5 large. The hypotheses were tested using multivariable logistic regression for binary dependent variables and Chi-squared tests for categorical dependent variables. The logistical and linear regressions were adjusted for a set of potential confounders. Variables for the multivariable models were selected using Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) according to theoretical considerations ( ). Nonparametric Cochran-Armitage statistics was used to test trend (i.e., hypothesis 2, increasing proportion of physiotherapists assessing with increasing education level). Contrast after an ANOVA was used to test whether the responsibility for screening was higher for physiotherapists as for other professions (hypothesis 5). An additional exploratory analysis was performed. i.e., it has been clearly stated that no a priori hypothesis was formulated and that this result needed to be interpreted with caution. The textual content of the semi-open questions (n=13) was analysed through a content analysis using an inductive approach ( ; ). This analysis approach was the most feasible due to the extensive data and the human resources available. Each free text response (meaning unit) was closely reviewed and summarised into main concepts (condensed meaning units). Those were then grouped into emerging themes making clinical or theoretical sense. To illustrate them, some participants' responses are provided verbatim in their original language. Finally, because there was some evidence of differences regarding fall risk activities and admission patterns to nursing home according to Swiss cantons ( ), it was decided to present the descriptive results stratified per language. Content analysis Open-ended questions (n=13) allowed participants to express themselves freely on different aspects related to fall risk assessment. The ideas underlying some of the themes are developed below, supported by verbatim quotes in their original language. All themes extracted from the analysis of these open-ended questions are presented in extended data “Extracted Themes” ( ). Other situations leading to fall risk assessment Other situations than those mentioned in the questionnaire may lead PTs to assess their patients' risk of falling. If this is not done during the initial assessment, the therapist might observe that the patient has balance problems when moving, exercising, or using walking aids. This may lead to a more detailed risk assessment. Return home after hospitalisation may also prompt PTs to assess the risk of falls of their patients. Other standardised assessments used Other assessments closely or remotely related to the risk of falls used by the PTs interviewed were: i) Functional Independence Measure (FIM), ii) Hierarchical Assessment of Balance and Mobility (HABAM), iii) Limit of stability test (LOS), iv) Modified Romberg Test (mRomberg), v) Multiple Sclerosis Questionnaire for Physiotherapists (MSQPT), vi) Romberg Test, and vii) The de Morton Mobility Index (DEMMI). Static balance assessment Static balance was assessed through various tests such as the One-Legged stance Test (OLST) or Single Leg Stance (SLS), or the 4-Stage Balance Scale Test. Some tests used such as the Berg Balance Scale (BBS) or the Balance Evaluation Systems Test (BESTest) examine both static and dynamic balance. PTs also mentioned testing balance on an unstable surface or with eyes closed without specifying whether this was done in a standardised way or not. Finally, the use of devices that also assess dynamic balance, such as the Huber 360 Evolution ® or the Galileo ® , was also stated. Participants who did not assess static balance gave reasons such as lack of knowledge, of specific tests, or of time during the initial assessment. For others, testing did not contribute to diagnosis and management and was therefore not considered necessary. A focus was placed on the reason for the initial consultation, thus favouring treatment over assessment. Some respondents said they did not trust the 0-5 manual muscle testing accuracy, which does not assess, for example, intra-muscular coordination. Other risk quantification Another way of quantifying the risk of falls was to follow the classification proposed by the test used. However, some participants pointed out that a fixed quantification of risk was impossible. Indeed, this one could depend on the use or not of walking aids, the fluctuation of the cognitive state, of the time of day, or of the environment. Other advice provided in relation to the risk of falls Advice regarding concentration during activities of daily living (ADL), foot sensitivity in diabetes, moving around at night, sedentary lifestyle and vestibular pathologies was also provided by PTs regarding fall risk. Other measures undertaken if the patient is at risk If a patient consulted for a reason other than rehabilitation to reduce the risk of falling and the assessment revealed that they were at risk, an additional measure undertaken was to encourage the patient to discuss this directly with their general practitioner. This helps to empower the patient while allowing them freedom to determine what measures they want to take (or not take) regarding this risk. Barriers against fall risk assessment Some barriers hindered some PTs from assess fall risk of their patients aged 65 and over for the risk of falling. One of these was the lack of sense in this approach. Indeed, a well-taken anamnesis, observation of the patient during exercises, during movements in the practice (waiting room - treatment room), when undressing or dressing, during functional exercises for example, or simply experience was according to them sufficient to assess the risk of falls. «Through history and functional tests and inspection in the assessment, the risk is identifiable. » (Translated from German to English by the authors.) «I believe that my experience is sufficient for an evaluation.” (Translated from French to English by the authors.) In addition, many patients were deemed not to be at risk because their gait seemed safe (observation), or they practiced a sport in their leisure time and might therefore find it questionable to assess their risk of falling. This led some therapists to focus on the initial reason for consultation mainly. Barriers against systematic fall risk assessment Barriers given against systematic assessment of patients over 65 are various. First, the age criterion alone was not sufficient to justify a systematic risk assessment according to some participants. 75-80 years old would be more appropriate for a so-called "systematic" assessment. In addition, this supplementary evaluation was perceived to be too time-consuming. "As I find the age limit for a systematic assessment of every patient of 65 years old too low, and we do not have the time and resources to clarify the risk of falls in all these patients regardless of the diagnoses and the A-Z. A large part of the patients I experience as still very fit and active at the age of 65." (Translated from German to English by the authors.) For some, a case-by-case approach would therefore be preferred in the first instance to a systematic procedure. The patient should be assessed according to his level of activity, his pathologies, his anamnesis, his antecedents, the subjective and objective assessment elements, of the general impression for example. However, other participants considered that everyone should be assessed because " prevention is better than cure ". Patients are often referred to PTs too late when the situation is already complex (generalised deconditioning, significant and/or disabling joint damage and cognitive disorders…). Discussion This online cross-sectional survey conducted in three language regions of Switzerland and including 938 participants aimed to investigate the current practices of physiotherapists in fall prevention. There were the main findings: i) 62% of physiotherapists perform a standardised fall risk assessment and most of them evaluate the different fall risk factors (e.g., balance or muscular strength). However, only 14% of physiotherapists working in an institutional context and 4% of those in a private practice carry it out in a systematic way. ii) The proportion of physiotherapists using a standardised risk assessment was higher in those with higher education compared to those with lower education, those working full time compared to those working part-time, in those working in teams compared to those working alone, and in those working in clinics or hospitals compared to those working in private practices. iii) Barriers to conducting a fall risk assessment were commonly a lack of technical resources, lack of theoretical knowledge, lack of time and lack of reimbursement. iv) Only 35% of the physiotherapists think that a systematic fall risk assessment of every new patient over 65 years of age should be implemented. v) The most frequent elements that would facilitate a more systematic fall risk assessment are the use of a quick and easy-to-use assessment tool, more time for the assessments and a checklist listing all the risk factors for falls to guide physiotherapists. Moreover, physiotherapists would like to see the establishment of uniform standardised procedures between the different health care providers in Switzerland. Current practices in assessing the risk of falls in patients over 65 years old Only 14% of physiotherapists working in an institutional context and 4% of those in a private practice used a standardised test or instrument to assess their patients' risk of falling in a systematic way (i.e., in at least 95% of their patients). Moreover, a disparity in the rate of assessment was also observable according to the initial pathologies (musculoskeletal, neurologic, respiratory). Annual assessment for the risk of falls among every patient 65 years of age or older is recommended ( ). In the light of our results, efforts are still needed to ensure that all patients over 65 are assessed by physiotherapists or other health care providers at least once a year. The implementation of a standardised risk assessment in physiotherapists with lower education, working in private practice, either alone or part-time, should notably be supported considering potential barriers. The Berg Balance Scale (BBS) and the Timed-Up and Go test (TUG) were the two most frequently assessments of fall risk used. Many physiotherapists also used the One-Legged Stance Test (OLST) or Single Leg Stance (SLS). These results were similarly observed in two other studies conducted in Australia and Canada with physiotherapists working in the geriatrics field ( ; ) suggesting that these tools are well known and implemented among physiotherapists. In their meta-analysis, Lusardi et al. , (2017) concluded that the BBS, the TUG and the Five Time Sit-To-Stand (FTSS) were the most evidence-supported functional measures to determine individual risk of future falls. However, a multifactorial assessment is required to evaluate the risk factors for falls ( ). It should be underlined that we did not analyse whether participants used these tools in isolation or combination. Generally, our results demonstrated a high level of involvement in assessing and advising on risk factors for falls. According literature, history of falls frequently showed a strong association with the risk of falls (odds ratios between 2.4 and 2.6) ( ). In line with these recommendations, 88.3% (n=655) of physiotherapists in Switzerland assess the history of falls. Another self-reported risk factor for falls is the perceived functional capacity. Indeed, showed that a poor consideration of self-general health increases the risk of falling (adjusted OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.14 to 4.42, p-value 0.019). This evaluation seems to be also well established among participants as 81% of them (n=595) asked their patients about their perceived functional capacity. In Switzerland, physiotherapists or pharmacists do not have any decision-making power regarding medication. Their common action would possibly be to contact the treating physician to see if certain medications could be removed or even replaced to avoid increasing the risk of falling. However, some collaborative projects between physiotherapists and pharmacists have been initiated in Switzerland. As part of its 100th anniversary, the Geneva Association of Physiotherapy decided to organise a campaign in collaboration with the Geneva pharmacists' association, Pharma Genève, on the theme: “Comment prévenir les chutes”. This campaign took place in the participating pharmacies from 25 September to 7 October 2017. The objective was to raise awareness of this risk that costs so much to society (and to our insurances) and above all the importance of maintaining physical activities whatever your age. Tests were carried out by pharmacy assistants, pharmacists and physiotherapists and advice on modifiable risk factors were given to the population ( ). More generally, in Switzerland, the standardisation of interprofessional collaboration, although supported, still faces many barriers (financial, lack of time). This kind of approach should be developed and strengthened in Switzerland, particularly in the prevention of falls ( ). It should also not to be forgotten that the use of screening tools can also carry certain risks. For example, if a screening test has moderate or low sensitivity and is applied in a population with a high incidence of falls. If the test is negative, there is a high risk that health care providers will mistakenly believe that the older person is not at increased risk of falls ( ). Barriers related to fall risk assessment According to our results, fall risk is often not assessed with a standardised approach. Indeed, one-quarter of physiotherapists (n=235, 25%) exclusively performed a subjective fall risk assessment mainly based on observation, anamnesis, or experience. Test-retest reliability may be lower in non-standardised tests than in standardised ones, making it less easy to reassess risk. Furthermore, this may result in the omission of some risk factors, which would be contrary to the recommendations of the guidelines in this area on multifactorial risk assessment ( ; ). Among the range of tools designed to standardise this procedure, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) developed the Stopping Elderly Accidents, Death and Injuries algorithm ( STEADI ). To screen for risk of falling, this valid instrument proposes the Stay Independent Brochure, a fall risk self-assessment tool, or the Three Key Questions, i) "Have you fallen in the last year?” ii) “Do you feel unsteady when standing or walking?” iii) “Do you worry about falling?”. If the patient is at risk, further assessments are provided to evaluate potential risk factors and define appropriate interventions ( ; ). The survey also highlighted other barriers like the lack of technical resources, theoretical knowledge, time, and financial recognition. Similar findings were made in studies evaluating the practices of fall risk assessment of patients by physiotherapists working with osteoarthritis patients (lack of time: 74%) ( ) or GPs (lack of time: 13.3%, of knowledge: 13.3%, of financial compensation: 11.1%) ( ). To address those issues, assessment of potential risk could be easily implemented using the Three Key Questions for example. Their application allowed 95% of patients at high risk to be identified while potentially decreasing the screening duration ( ). Finally, only 35% of physiotherapists stated that systematic fall risk assessment should be performed. The notion of systematic implies “every new patient over 65 years of age”. Several participants stated that the age of 65 was not appropriate due to the heterogeneity of patients in this age group, stating that 75-80 years would be more appropriate for a systematic procedure. However, if we look at the Swiss statistics on falls during the year 2017, we can see that the proportion of fallers increases by 10% between people aged 65-79 and those over 80 ( ). This demonstrates the importance of fall risk assessment at an early stage. Clinical implications Despite the multitude of tests available, many participants would like a quick and easy-to-use assessment tool or a checklist listing all the risk factors for falls to guide them in assessing patients over 65 years old. The implementation in Switzerland of a tool directly targeting fall risk assessment such as the STEADI algorithm, could be relevant. Indeed, it was specially created to help caregivers to perform fall risk assessments and treat patients appropriately ( ). Physiotherapists working in private practice, either alone or part-time, should particularly be supported to use standardised assessments. Improvements in basic education, continuing education courses, online materials, financial incentives (i.e., remuneration for assessments), and interprofessional prevention campaigns could also potentially increase the implementation of established best practices in fall prevention. In addition, many therapists called for the standardisation of current practices between different health care providers. This would enable the adoption of a "common language" in terms of testing, risk quantification and interventions. According to Gaboreau et al. 65.3% of French GPs considered the implementation of an annual falls risk assessment useful. Unfortunately, only 28.8% of them performed it each year ( ). To optimise practices related to falls prevention, it is therefore essential to increase the awareness and involvement of each health professional. More generally, there is still room for improvement in the quality of care, coordination between the treating physician and the specialist, and follow-up care after discharge from hospital in Switzerland ( ). Future studies Future studies are needed to develop a fall risk assessment adapted to the needs and constraints of physiotherapist’s practice in Switzerland. This tool could be based on the STEADI, which was proven to reduce falls-related hospital admissions in older people and associated health care costs ( ). Then, local implementation studies including in-depth qualitative interviews with sub-groups of physiotherapists to identify potential barriers and facilitators could be planned. This tool could thus serve as a basis for discussion and joint decision-making among health professionals. Limitations Participant’s recruitment One limitation was, that we could no address all, or a random sampling of all physiotherapists working in Switzerland. In the absence of a federal register comprising all currently practising physiotherapists in Switzerland, a recruitment strategy was developed to maximise the results generalisability and sample representativeness. The research team sent more than 3600 emails and the partner associations and schools to set up our sample. However, this strategy did not avoid the phenomenon of overlapping; obviously, some physiotherapists have been contacted in several ways while others were omitted. Moreover, physiotherapists who took part may have been more sensitive to this topic than non-respondents, potentially influencing the results. The generalisation of cross-sectional survey findings is often discussed in the literature. For some authors, sources of disparity within the population studied do not allow the results to be generalised between the individuals contacted and the others ( ). For others, due to the large number of individuals contacted, this design is more likely than others to acquire data from a representative sample and thus allow extrapolation ( ). We assumed that our sample is representative of all physiotherapists working in Switzerland but are not able to test this and therefore these findings should be interpreted with caution. Nonetheless, this study provides a snapshot of the current global situation in Switzerland regarding fall risk assessment, considering that the physiotherapist's practices and knowledge are in constant evolution. Without pretending to fulfil the criteria of a mixed design, but to allow participants to specify or clarify their answers, twelve open-ended questions were also asked. The analysis of the participants' answers was limited to a content analysis based on the inductive approach proposed by Elo and Kyngäs and Graneheim and Lundman ( ; ). This work, although long and tedious, was fascinating. It raised relevant aspects concerning the needs of physiotherapists and the future reflections to be carried out to prevent falls in our country. However, it would have been relevant to carry out this work with the help of a third person to ensure that the answers were well understood and that the classification by themes was adequate and unanimous. Strengths First, to our knowledge, it is the first study to explore this topic in Switzerland. Fall prevention is of high importance to improve the care of our older patients. Guidelines have underlined the effectiveness of multifactorial assessment to determine an individual’s risk of falling and implement suitable prevention strategies ( ; ; ; ; ). It was, therefore, necessary to review current practices and to propose measures according to physiotherapists needs. Furthermore, our recruitment strategy and the development of a questionnaire in three languages (French, German, Italian) enabled nationwide participation, with the final sample size exceeding our initial expectations. In addition, this study led some participants to reflect on their current practices. Conclusions In conclusion, this study showed that most physiotherapists working in Switzerland perform some form of fall risk assessment. Moreover, many of them are aware of the problem as they frequently assess and advise on risk factors for falls to their patients over 65 years old. However, despite current recommendations, risk assessment itself is still too often unsystematic and based on subjective criteria. Measures are required to foster the use of standardised assessments by mitigating existing barriers and increasing incentives. To overcome this challenge, education plays an important role and should emphasise the importance of objective fall risk assessments with the use of appropriate screening tools. In addition, the development of an assessment to facilitate the implementation of a fall prevention strategy based on best practice should be considered. This would improve adequate care for our older adults while relieving the health system of the costs associated with this issue. Introduction As the sixth most common cancer and the third leading cause of cancer-related death, liver cancer is a global health problem with high incidence rates, especially in Asian and African countries [ , , ]. The treatment of liver cancers encounters many difficulties due to the rapidly proliferative and aggressive nature of the disease [ ]. In addition, the pathogenic mechanisms of liver cancers are numerous and complicated, and the strategies for treating live cancers are strictly dependent on the stage of tumor and liver functions [ ]. The above-mentioned findings point out the predicament of liver cancer in tailored medical therapy [ ]. Accordingly, the overall prognosis of liver cancer is poor, with a 5-year survival rate less than 20% [ ]. Although many methods have been adopted for liver cancer treatment, such as surgery, transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE), radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and targeted medicines, the efficacy of these treatments remains very limited in advanced liver cancer [ ]. In recent decades, cancer immunotherapy has become recognized as a highly anticipated strategy for cancer therapy [ , ]. The investigation of therapeutic approaches such as adoptive cell immunotherapy, for instance, chimeric antigen receptor T cells and T cell receptor engineered T cells for liver cancers, are developing rapidly [ ]. In addition, many investigators have dedicated their research to developing immune checkpoint inhibitors that can relieve immune checkpoint blockage and restore immune activity against tumors [ , ]. Various approved immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as ipilimumab against T lymphocyte CTLA-4 and nivolumab/pembrolizumab against T lymphocyte PD-1, have been widely used in treatment for liver cancer [ , , ]. However, inhibition of immune checkpoints during ipilimumab, nivolumab, or pembrolizumab treatment often causes adverse events such as hepatitis, dermatitis, pancreatitis, pneumonitis, enteritis, and arthritis [ ]. In liver cancer patients receiving immunotherapy, autoimmune disorders such as type 1 diabetes mellitus, myasthenia gravis, and rheumatoid arthritis have been reported [ ]. Escitalopram oxalate (Lexapro ® ) is a superior SSRI used to treat major depressive disorder (MDD) and anxiety, and has revealed favorable tolerability and less adverse symptoms in various randomized and double-blind controlled studies [ , ]. Recently, mounting evidence has indicated the anticancer potentials of escitalopram oxalate [ , , , , ]. Indeed, escitalopram oxalate has been demonstrated to inhibit the proliferation of GBM cells [ , ] and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells [ ] by inducing apoptosis or autophagy. Similar results were reported in a nationwide population-based study, indicating that administration of escitalopram oxalate is associated with decreased HCC risk [ ]. Moreover, a very recent study involving both bench work and a nationwide population-based cohort study reported that escitalopram oxalate inhibits the proliferation of liver cancer cells by inducing autophagy and that its use involves a reduced HCC risk [ ]. Chemotherapy and immunotherapy in anticancer treatment may cause various adverse events. such as drug resistance and toxicity, leading to a negative impact on therapeutic efficacy [ ]. Notably, a systematic review and pooled analysis have both noted that combinational treatments of immunotherapy and chemotherapy exhibit encouraging anti-tumor potential and an acceptable toxicity profile in patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer [ ]. Therefore, combinational use of multiple anticancer drugs may improve treatment efficacy by inducing synergistic effects and overcoming adverse influences such as drug resistance and toxicity [ ]. Because escitalopram oxalate has been reported to have potential against several cancers, the current study adopted combinational use of low-dose escitalopram oxalate and nivolumab to verify the resulting synergistic inhibitory potential against liver cancer both in vitro and in vivo. 2. Discussion Nivolumab (Opdivo ® ), known as an anticancer drug belonging to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI), is a fully human immunoglobulin G4 monoclonal anti-body against programmed cell death receptor 1 (PD-1) [ ]. The action mechanism of nivolumab is to disrupt the signaling of the PD-1 immune checkpoint and thereby recover the anticancer activity of suppressed effector T cells [ ]. In recent decades, evidence has indicated that nivolumab can be used widely for treatment of various cancers, including liver cancer [ , ]. Nivolumab can cause T-cell activation by blocking immune checkpoints and elect autoimmune toxicities, which leads to tumor destruction [ ]. However, evidence has indicated that single ICI does not meet the expected goals [ , ]. Indeed, worse treatment-associated side effects or common grade 3 adverse events such as pal-mar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia, elevated aspartate aminotransferase, and hypertension were revealed in a randomized multicenter open-label, phase 3 clinical trial of patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma [ ]. In addition, nivolumab has shown increased risk of various immune-related adverse events such as maculopapular rash, pneumonitis, hepatitis, and infusion-related reactions, suggesting a higher risk when increasing the dosage of nivolumab [ , ]. Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy has emerged as a rising star in cancer treatment. However, despite the success of ICIs, the issue of resistance to ICIs restricts the patients able to achieve durable responses, which has been a major concern [ ]. Recent clinical trials such as KEYNOTE-240 and CheckMate 459 in HCC treatment did not achieve their predefined goals for overall survival [ ]. Additionally, resistance to ICI treatment, including nivolumab, has been reported in cancers such as ovarian cancer, renal cell carcinoma, and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma [ , , ]. Therefore, the combination of ICIs with other therapies, such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), chemotherapy, or local therapy, is commonly considered and adopted in cancer therapy [ ]. Accordingly, the current study reports that combinational use of nivolumab and escitalopram oxalate exhibits a synergistic effect on inhibiting the proliferation of HepG2 cells in vitro and in a xenograft HepG2 tumor animal model. These findings may provide an alternative option for liver cancer treatment. Escitalopram oxalate is an anti-depressive reagent exhibiting favorable tolerability and less adverse clinical events [ , ]. In recent decades, administration of escitalopram oxalate has been found to have a negative correlation with various kinds of cancers, such as bladder cancer, renal cancer, and liver cancer [ , , ]. Similar results have been reported in bench work, noting that escitalopram oxalate inhibits the proliferation of non-small-cell lung cancer cells and brain cancer cells [ , ]. A very recent study indicated the protective effect of escitalopram oxalate on liver cancer via induction of autophagy [ ]. In addition, no adverse event was reported by daily administration of 600 mg escitalopram oxalate [ ]. Another study reported that an antibiotic regimen containing escitalopram oxalate reveals synergistic inhibitory effects on growth of multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria [ ]. Indeed, these findings may provide reasonable suggestions that escitalopram oxalate is a favorable option for inclusion in a regimen for HCC treatment. However, further investigations and clinical trials are merited to verify the curative effects of combinational use of nivolumab and escitalopram oxalate on treatment of liver cancer.
